messages.subject: Re: [seewave] Splliting a spectrogram
messages.body_plain:
Dear Vincent,

Yes, because by definition the zone you zoom in has not the same number of FFT windows, so the time dimension is changed. 'tlim' operates as a zoom not as a selection (trim) tool.

Two solutions below, but none is really nice I must confess:

HTH

Jerome

library(seewave)
data(tico)

############
## solution #1
############
tlim <- c(0.5,1)
d <- duration(tico)
sel <- cutw(tico, from=tlim[1], to=tlim[2], output="Wave")
sel <- addsilw(sel, at="start", d=tlim[1], output="Wave")
sel <- addsilw(sel, at="end", d=d-tlim[2], output="Wave")

png("full-selection-trim.png")
par(mfrow=c(2,1))
spectro(tico, scale=FALSE)
spectro(sel, scale=FALSE)
dev.off()

############
## solution #2
############
png("full-selection-margins.png")
par(mfrow=c(2,1), mar=c(3, 4, 1, 1))
spectro(tico, scale=FALSE, tlab="")
par(mar=c(4.5, 12, 1, 14))
spectro(tico, tlim=tlim, scale=FALSE)
dev.off()

De: "Vincent M, LBBE" <vincent...@gmail.com>
À: "seewave GROUP" <see...@googlegroups.com>
Envoyé: Vendredi 31 Janvier 2020 15:40:51
Objet: [seewave] Splliting a spectrogram

Hi jérôme,

We want to split a spectrogram such that we get one spectrogram per syllable of a sound (we have the syllables coordinates).

We used "spectro" function with the option "tlim" and the syllables coordinates. It works but... it turns out that these "local" spectrograms are not exactly the same that when we plot the whole spectrogram... In other word, looking at the whole spectrogram or looking at a local spectrogram, we don't have the same image...

Is there a way to obtain exactly the same spectrogram image when we look at the whole or part of the spectrogram?

Many thanks, et merci

Vincent M, LBBE LYON

--

messages.subject: segment function imprecise
messages.body_plain:
I am working on gecko vocalisations, which are short (~22 ms) pulses of sound. One of the variables I am interested in, is pulse length, and I have used function "segment" to do this (including other things), since "syllables" is one of the outputs. However, when I compare the measurements taken with those I do manually in Audacity, they are almost always longer (using segment), quite inconsistent, and seem to be highly imprecise - I get only 2 different numbers repeated (e.g:
23.21995
23.21995
23.21995
34.82993
34.82993
34.82993
34.82993
23.21995
), for a set of 8 different geckos with considerable variation in their pulse length, which indicates to me that all the variation between those numbers is being ignored. I can't see why that is, as it should be fairly simple when working with a vector of amplitudes to find the start and end of a syllable with a specified minimum amplitude. Any idea what I can do to fix this?

I have attached some sound files, and the code I used:

#############################################################
##Packages:
require(soundgen)
require(seewave)
require(tuneR)

## Set the location of the files to be analysed and make list of the files

file.lst = list.files("[file location here]")

###########################################################################################
##  convert Wav files to Wave objects (TuneR)

waves = lapply(file.lst, function(x){
  readWave(x)
})

###########################################################################################
## filter out frequencies below 0.9 kHz (mostly noise)
## converting wave to vector

wavesF = lapply(waves, function(x){
  ffilter(x, from = 0, to = 900, bandpass = F,
          wl = 512, ovlp = 0,
          output = "matrix")
})

###########################################################################################
## Make spectogram of filtered sound using seewave

spcgrm = lapply(wavesF, function(x){
  spec(x, f = 44100, wl = 512, ovlp = 0, plot =  F)})

###########################################################################################
##  calculates the amplitudes for the frequency-filtered noise

amplts = lapply(wavesF, function(x){
  env(x, f = 44100, msmooth = c(512, 0), norm = T,
      plot = F)
})

##########################################################################################
##  set the syllable threshold value at a standard, normalised to the loudest 2%
#    of the call (rather than normalising to the mean amplitude of the whole sound,
#    which is the default for function "segment" below, and causes too much vairability)

# scaling factor: mean amplitude of top 2%
SF = lapply(amplts, function(x)
{mean(na.omit(tail(sort(x), (nrow(x)/50))))})

# syllable threshold for segmentation ("segment" below), normalising
# mean amplitude to SF:
ST = lapply(1:(length(file.lst)), function(x){
  SF[[x]]/5/mean(amplts[[x]], na.rm = T)
})

###########################################################################################
##  Segment the sound into syllables using normalised threshold value (ST)

seg = lapply(1:(length(file.lst)), function(x){
  segment(wavesF[[x]][,1], samplingRate = 44100,
          windowLength = (512/44.1),
          overlap = 0, shortestSyl = 8,
          sylThres = ST[[x]], shortestPause = 40,
          plot = T, main = file.lst[[x]]
  )})

#median pulse length (milliseconds):
PLmd = lapply(seg, function(x){median(x$syllables$sylLen)})

PLmd #the list of median pulse lengths for each file

messages.subject: Acustica data comparison
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
I just started working with acoustic data on killer whales in R, I'm a beginner in this field.
What's the best way to compare 2 sounds seeking similarity? Should I compare oscillograms or rather spectrograms?

Ant advice is appreciated,
Thanks,
Stefano

messages.subject: Re: Acustica data comparison
messages.body_plain:
Hi Stephano

Spectograms would be the way to go. You can look into machine-learning algorithms to group similar calls based on spectograms. For a basic and more manual approach, I would recommend using Audacity (free) to analyse the calls. You could also look into the many bioaccoustic programs that are also free (such as Raven), although Audacity generally gives you more options as it is designed for sound in general.
